title: Role of FDFT1 polymorphism for fibrosis progression in patients with chronic hepatitis C.
text_summary: 本研究旨在评估FDFT1基因多态性与慢性丙型肝炎（CHC）患者脂肪变性、纤维化进展及抗病毒治疗反应之间的关系。通过实时PCR检测478例接受聚乙二醇干扰素α-2a/利巴韦林治疗的CHC患者（男性314例，女性164例，平均年龄44.9±10.7岁，GT1型387例，GT4型91例）的rs738409478和rs2645424位点。结果显示，FDFT1 rs2645424位点的基因型分布为GG：186（38.9%）、AG：222（46.4%）和AA：70（14.6%），PNPLA3 rs738409位点的基因型分布为CC：269（56.3%）、CG：177（37.0%）和GG：32（6.7%）。总体而言，FDFT1多态性与脂肪变性和纤维化程度无关。然而，在无脂肪变性患者中，AA基因型与进展期纤维化相关（AA：8/20（40.0%），AG：6/70（8.5%），GG：9/57（16.1%），P=0.003）。相反，较小的PNPLA3等位基因与脂肪变性和进展期纤维化相关（P<0.001）。这两个SNP对治疗反应没有影响。结论：FDFT1的较小等位基因与非脂肪变性亚组的进展期纤维化相关，但与脂肪变性亚组无关。这表明脂肪变性和非脂肪变性CHC患者的纤维化进展可能存在不同的代谢途径。

VIRAL HEPATITIS
Role of FDFT1 polymorphism for ﬁbrosis progression in patients with
chronic hepatitis C
Albert F. St€attermayer1, Karoline Rutter1, Sandra Beinhardt1, Fritz Wrba2, Thomas-Matthias Scherzer1,
Michael Strasser3, Harald Hofer1, Petra Steindl-Munda1, Michael Trauner1 and Peter Ferenci1
1 Department of Internal Medicine III, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Medical University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria
2 Department of Clinical Pathology, Medical University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria
3 Department of Internal Medicine I, Paracelsus Medical Private University, Salzburg, Austria
Keywords
Chronic hepatitis C – FDFT1 – ﬁbrosis –
PNPLA3 – steatosis
Abbreviations
CHC, Chronic hepatitis C; EVR, early
virological response; FDFT1, farnesyl
diphosphate farnesyl transferase 1; GT,
genotype; HCV, hepatitis C virus; IL28B,
interleukin 28B; PEG, peg-interferon-a-2a;
PNPLA3, patatin-like phospholipase domain-
containing 3; RBV, ribavirin; RVR, rapid
virological response; SNP, single nucleotide
polymorphism; SVR, sustained virological
response.
Correspondence
Prof. Dr. Peter Ferenci, Department of
Internal Medicine III, Division for
Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Medical
University of Vienna, W€ahringer G€urtel 18-20
A-1090 Vienna, Austria
Tel: +43 1 40 400 4735
Fax: +43 1 40 400 4741
e-mail: peter.ferenci@meduniwien.ac.at
Received 8 May 2013
Accepted 17 June 2013
DOI:10.1111/liv.12269
Liver Int. 2014: 34: 388–395
Abstract
Background: In chronic hepatitis C (CHC), steatosis is associated with ﬁbro-
sis and impaired response to antiviral therapy. Recently, a polymorphism of
single nucleotide polymorphism SNP rs2645424 of farnesyl diphosphate
farnesyl transferase 1 (FDFT1) was identiﬁed in NAFLD/NASH as a possible
causal link to steatosis and ﬁbrosis progression. SNP rs738409 in the adi-
ponutrin gene (PNPLA3) is a well described factor for steatosis. This study
evaluated the relation of these SNPs on steatosis, ﬁbrosis and treatment
response in CHC. Methods: The SNPs rs738409478 and rs2645424 were
determined by real-time PCR in 478 patients with CHC (m/f: 314/164; mean
age: 44.9 ± 10.7; GT1: 387, GT4: 91) who completed treatment with peg-
IFN-a-2a/ribavirin. All had a pretreatment liver biopsy. Steatosis and ﬁbrosis
were graded by board-certiﬁed pathologists according to Brunt and META-
VIR respectively. Results: The distribution of FDFT1 rs2645424 was GG: 186
(38.9%), AG: 222 (46.4%) and AA: 70 (14.6%) and of the rs738409 PNPLA3
allele: CC: 269 (56.3%), CG: 177 (37.0%) and GG: 32 (6.7%).
Overall,
FDTF1 polymorphism was not linked to the extent of steatosis or ﬁbrosis.
However, in patients without steatosis the AA genotype was associated with
advanced ﬁbrosis [AA: 8/20 (40.0%), AG: 6/70 (8.5%), GG: 9/57 (16.1%),
P = 0.003]. In contrast, the minor PNPLA3 allele was associated with both
steatosis and advanced ﬁbrosis (P < 0.001).
Both SNPs did not inﬂuence
treatment response. Conclusion: The minor allele in FDFT1 was associated
with advanced ﬁbrosis in the non-steatotic but not in the steatotic subgroup.
This may reﬂect different metabolic pathways in ﬁbrosis progression for stea-
totic and non-steatotic patients with CHC.
Chronic hepatitis C (CHC) is one of the most common
blood-borne viral infections, accounting for almost 170
million infected subjects worldwide, and is one of the
leading causes for liver-related mortality. Hepatic stea-
tosis is found in more than half of the infected patients
and is associated with faster progression of ﬁbrosis to
cirrhosis (1) and lack of treatment response to antiviral
treatment (2). Still, the causes and pathogenetic mecha-
nisms for steatosis development and ﬁbrosis progression
are not well understood; both, host and viral factors are
discussed.
Several genetic risk factors for steatosis haven been
identiﬁed so far, the best documented one is a
single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in rs738409 in
the
patatin-like
phospholipase
domain-containing-3
(PNPLA3) gene on chromosome 22. This polymor-
phism is associated with the severity of liver damage in
patients with non-genotype-3 chronic hepatitis C (3, 4).
The impact of PNPLA3 on treatment outcome in CHC
patients is controversial: Valenti et al. showed higher
SVR rates in difﬁcult-to-cure patients (genotypes 1 and
4, advanced ﬁbrosis) carrying the beneﬁcial C allele (5).
On the other hand, in the study by Trepo et al. no asso-
ciation between SVR and PNPLA3 was observed (3). A
genome-wide association study (GWAS) identiﬁed an
SNP in the farnesyl diphosphate farnesyl transferase 1
(FDFT1) gene region (rs2645424) on chromosome 8p23
(6) which was associated with the NAFLD activity score

388

(NAS) in non-hispanic white women with NAFLD.
Additionally,
another
study
found
an
association
between FDFT1 with the stage of ﬁbrosis, but not with
the degree of steatosis, lobular inﬂammation, ballooning
or NAS (7). FDFT1 encodes for a squalene synthase that
catalyzes the production of squalene from farnesyl pyro-
phosphate as the ﬁrst step in the sterol biosynthesis
pathway (8). These ﬁndings might suggest a potential
role of dysregulated cholesterol metabolism in the pro-
gression from steatosis to NASH (9) and further in the
development of ﬁbrosis. Furthermore, Tillmann et al.
showed an association between IL28B CC genotype and
the absence of steatosis in two CHC cohorts (10). This
association could not be observed by Valenti et al., but
on the other hand in PNPLA3 non GG patients, subjects
with
IL28B
CC
had
signiﬁcantly
higher
rates
of
advanced ﬁbrosis (5).
The aim of our study was to evaluate the inﬂuence of
FDFT1 on steatosis development, ﬁbrosis progression
and virological response to peg-interferon-a-2a/ribavi-
rin standard-of-care treatment in genotype 1 and 4
treatment-naive CHC patients.
Methods
Study population
A total of 478 consecutive treatment-naive patients (314
male, 164 female) with chronic hepatitis C (GT1: 387,
GT4: 91) from eight Austrian tertiary referral centres,
who completed a full course of antiviral treatment with
peg-IFN-a-2a and RBV between 2003 and 2011, were
included in this study and analysed retrospectively. The
institutional review board approved this retrospective,
non-interventional analysis.
This study included 251 subjects, who participated in
a published randomized controlled trial for response
guided therapy in GT1 and 4 infected patients (11, 12).
The remaining 227 patients were treated according to
the label (peg-IFN-a-2a 180 lg/week and RBV 1000–
1200 mg/day for 24–72 weeks). The primary efﬁcacy
outcome was SVR, deﬁned as undetectable HCV-RNA
24 weeks after end of the treatment. On treatment, viro-
logical
response
was
deﬁned
as
rapid
virological
response [RVR; HCV-RNA below limit of detection
(LOD) after 4 weeks of treatment], complete early viro-
logical response (cEVR; HCV-RNA below LOD after
12 weeks of treatment) and end-of-treatment response
(EoT; HCV-RNA below LOD at the end of treatment).
Non-response was deﬁned as detectable HCV-RNA at
treatment week 24 or less than 2log10-drop after
12 weeks on treatment.
Patients with a liver disease other than hepatitis C as
well as patients with ongoing alcohol abuse (>50 g/day)
or with viral co-infection (HBV, HIV) were excluded
from the study. Patients infected with genotype 2 or 3
were also not eligible. Anthropometric data like age
(years), body weight (kg) and height (cm) were
collected and body mass index (BMI; kg/m2) was calcu-
lated for each patient. All patients consented for liver
biopsy and genetic testing.
Testing for serum hepatitis C virus RNA
HCV-RNA was quantiﬁed in all patients at baseline and
after 4, 12, 24, 48 and 72 weeks of treatment and
24 weeks after end of the treatment.
For detection of Serum HCV-RNA, the COBAS
Amplicor HCV Test (Roche Molecular Systems; Branch-
burg, NJ, USA; LOD: <50 IU/ml); for quantiﬁcation we
used the COBAS Amplicor HCV Monitor Test (limit of
quantiﬁcation [LOQ]: <500 IU/ml) and from 2007
onward the COBAS AmpliPrep/COBAS TaqMan HCV
Test (Roche Diagnostocs; Pleasanton, CA, USA; LOQ:
<15 IU/ml). The HCV genotype was determined by
using the VERSANT HCV Genotype 2.0 Assay (LiPA)
(Siemens Medical Solutions Diagnostics; Tarrytown,
NY, USA). All assays were performed according to the
manufacturers’ instructions.
Genetic testing
Single
nucleotide
polymorphisms
from
rs12979860
(IL28B), rs738409 (PNPLA3) and rs2645424 (FDFT1)
were analysed by using the StepOnePlus Real Time PCR
Systems (Applied Biosystems; Foster City, CA, USA)
with a TaqMan SNP Genotyping Assay developed
together with Applied Biosystems using published
sequences from the NCBI Entrez SNP Database (www.
ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/entrez). All patients consented
for genetic testing.
Liver biopsies
All liver biopsies were performed within 2 years prior
to treatment initiation and read by board-certiﬁed
pathologists at each centre unaware of the clinical and
laboratory data of the patients. Biopsy samples were
routinely
processed
(formalin-ﬁxed
and
parafﬁn-
embedded) and stained with haematoxylin/eosin and
chrome aniline blue for assessment of ﬁbrosis, steatosis
and inﬂammation as well as with Prussian blue iron
stain.
Fibrosis and necroinﬂammatory activity was staged
according to the METAVIR-Score: no ﬁbrosis (F0), por-
tal ﬁbrosis without septa (F1), portal ﬁbrosis with few
septa (F2), numerous septa without cirrhosis (F3) and
cirrhosis (F4). The necroinﬂammatory activity was
graded as absent (A0), mild (A1), moderate (A2) and
severe (A3) inﬂammation (13).
Steatosis was semiquantiﬁed only in 360 patients
(treated at two centres) by the four-point scale accord-
ing to Brunt (14) by calculating the percentage of lipid
containing hepatocytes of the total number of hepato-
cytes at a 409 magniﬁcation: G0 (<5%); G1 (up to
33%), G2 (34 to 66%) and G3 (>66%).

Biochemical assessment
Blood samples were obtained at baseline of antiviral
therapy under fasting conditions and measured by stan-
dard laboratory techniques. Total serum cholesterol
[upper limit of normal (ULN): 190 mg/dl], triglycerides
(ULN: 172 mg/dl), blood glucose (ULN: 100 mg/dl),
alanin (ALT, ULN: 45 U/L) and aspartate transaminases
(AST, ULN: 35 U/L) were determined.
Statistical analysis
Categorical variables were expressed as absolute and
relative frequencies. Continuous variables were shown
as median and interquartile range (IQR). Continuous
variables were compared using the analysis of variance
(ANOVA) for Gaussian distributions or the Kruskall–Wal-
lis test for non-Gaussian distributions. Gaussian distri-
bution was evaluated with the Kolmogorow–Smirnow
test. For categorical variables, we used the Pearson’s v²-
test or the Fisher’s exact test, where appropriate. All tests
were two-sided and a P-value below 0.05 was considered
as signiﬁcant. For further analysis, we performed a mul-
tivariable logistic regression model to identify indepen-
dent factors associated with steatosis, ﬁbrosis and
treatment response.
All statistical analyses were performed with commer-
cially available software (SPSS Version 20, IBM Corp.,
Chicago, IL, USA).
Results
In total, 478 patients were analysed. Of those, 65.7%
(n = 314) were male, 34.3% (n = 164) were female. The
majority [n = 387 (81.0%)] were infected with genotype
1, 91 patients (9.0%) were infected with genotype 4.
Mean age was 44.9 ± 10.7 years and mean BMI was
25.6 ± 3.9 kg/m². Exactly, 183 (38.3%) patients were
homozygous C allele carriers in rs738409 (PNPLA3),
177 (37.0%) were heterozygotes and 32 (6.7%) had the
GG genotype. Corresponding ﬁgures for SNPs in
rs2645424 (FDFT1) were 186 (38.9% GG), 222 (46.4%)
AG and 70 (14.6%) AA. 161 patients (33.7%) had the
beneﬁcial CC genotype in rs12979860 (IL28B), 251
(52.5%) were heterozygotes and 66 (13.8%) were homo-
zygous T allele carriers. Patients with genotype 4 were
more likely to be male, were signiﬁcantly younger, had
higher BMI, lower baseline viral load, lower AST levels
and a higher rate of RVR. All demographic data are
summarized in Table 1.
Factors associated with steatosis
Steatosis was quantiﬁed in 360 patients (75.3%). The
median
percentage
was
5%
with
an
interquartile
range (IQR) from 0 to 20%. Steatosis (≥5% of
hepatocytes) was observed in 213 patients (59.1%)
and 36 (10.0%) had moderate- to- severe steatosis
(G2 or 3; ≥33% of hepatocytes). A total of 147
(40.8%) of the patients had no signiﬁcant steatosis
(G0; <5% of hepatocytes).
The SNP rs2645424 polymorphism within the FDFT1
gene did not correlate with the presence or extent of
steatosis: 5% (0–15%) in AA vs. 5% (0–20%) in AG vs.
10% (0–20%) in GG (P = 0.952). Rates of moderate/
severe steatosis were similarly distributed across the
three genotypes [AA: n = 4/54 (7.4%); AG: n = 22/166
(13.3%); GG: n = 10/140 (7.1%); P = 0.163].
In contrast, the rs738409 PNPLA3 polymorphism
was predictive for steatosis. Patients carrying the GG
allele had signiﬁcantly higher percentage of steatosis
[20% (IQR: 10–35%)] than patients with CG [10% (0–
20%), P = 0.001] or CC [5% (0–15%), P < 0.001]. For
further analysis, patients with CG or CC were evaluated
together.
No
steatosis
(<5%
of
hepatocytes)
was
observed in 43.3% (n = 145/335) of patients carrying
the C allele but only in 8.0% (n = 2/25) of the GG carri-
ers (P < 0.001). Furthermore, moderate- to- severe stea-
tosis (Grade 2 or 3) was more common in GG patients
[n = 6/25 (24.0%)] than in C allele carriers [n = 30/335
(9.0%); P = 0.028].
Steatosis was also more pronounced in patients carry-
ing the T allele of rs12979860 IL28B than in those with
CC [10% (0–20%) vs. 5% (0–14%); P = 0.019]. T allele
carriers tended to have a higher rate of moderate/severe
steatosis [n = 27/236 (11.4%)] than CC carriers [n = 9/
124 (7.3%)], but without reaching a level of signiﬁcance
(P = 0.268).
Among non-genetic
factors, steatosis was more
common in obese [BMI>30 kg/m²: 20% (5–30%)]
than in overweighted [25–30 kg/m²: 10% (4–25%)]
or
in
normal
weighted
patients
[<25 kg/m²:
5%
(0–10%), P < 0.001]. Steatosis was less common in
younger patients [<40 years: 4% (0–10%)] than in
patients over 40 years [10% (4–20%), P < 0.001].
HCV genotype, viral load and gender had no impact
on steatosis.

m²-increment;

1.159–2.088;
P = 0.003), age (>40y; OR: 2.384, CI 95%: 1.431–3.973;

and
PNPLA3

neither associated with triglyceride levels [AA: 109

Factors associated with ﬁbrosis stage
Fibrosis stage was evaluated in 478 patients, of whom
156 (32.6%) subjects had advanced ﬁbrosis deﬁned as
bridging ﬁbrosis (F3) or cirrhosis (F4). 18.0% (n = 86)
had liver biopsy proven signs of cirrhosis (F4).
In the overall study cohort, FDFT1 was not associated
with the stage of ﬁbrosis; advanced ﬁbrosis was equally
distributed across the different genotypes in rs2645424:
34.3% (n = 24/70) of AA, 33.8% (n = 75/222) of AG
and
30.6%
(n = 57/186)
of
GG
allele
carriers
(P = 0.758) had advanced ﬁbrosis (F3–4). When the
analysis was restricted to patients without steatosis (G0;
n = 147), advanced ﬁbrosis was higher in patients with
AA [40.0% (n = 8/20)] compared to patients with AG
[8.6% (n = 6/70)] or GG [15.8% (n = 9/57); P = 0.003;
Fig. 1]. After adjustment for sex, age, BMI, HCV geno-
type, viral load, PNPLA3, cholesterol and triglycerides,
only age (>40y; OR: 9.967, CI 95%: 2.098–47.340;
P = 0.004) and FDFT1 genotype (AA; OR: 6.944, CI
95%: 2.083–23.256; P = 0.002) were independently
associated with advanced ﬁbrosis. In patients with mild
steatosis (G1; n = 177), advanced ﬁbrosis was more
common in patients with AG [52.7% (n = 39/74)] and
GG [39.7% (n = 29/73)], than in homozygous A carri-
ers [29.4% (n = 8/30); P = 0.040]. No differences in
rates of advanced ﬁbrosis were observed in the subgroup
with moderate/severe steatosis (G2–3; n = 36): AA:
50.0% (n = 2/2), AG: 59.1% (n = 13/22) and GG:
40.0% (n = 4/10); P = 0.601. Genotypes of FDFT1 were
equally distributed across the different subgroups:
minor allele frequency was 38.1% in patients without
steatosis, 37.4% in mild steatosis and 41.7% in moder-
ate/severe steatosis respectively.
Homozygous GG allele rs738409 (PNPLA3) carriers
had a higher rate [56.3% (n = 18/32)] of advanced
ﬁbrosis than patients carrying the C allele [30.9%
(n = 138/446),
P = 0.003].
In
contrast,
rates
of
advanced ﬁbrosis did not differ in patients with CC or
T allele in rs12979860 IL28B [32.9% (n = 53/161) vs.
32.5% (n = 103/317) respectively; P = 0.925].
Patients older than 40 years had a higher rate of
advanced ﬁbrosis [41.8% (n = 136/325)] than patients
younger
than
40 years
[13.1%
(n = 20/153),
P < 0.001]. No association between HCV genotype, sex
and BMI could be observed.
Multivariate logistic regression identiﬁed PNPLA3
(GG; OR: 3.534, CI 95%: 1.538–8.130; P = 0.003), older
age (>40y; OR: 5.143, CI 95%: 2.906–9.103; P < 0.001)
and low cholesterol (continuous; OR: 0.992, CI 95%:
0.986–0.998; P = 0.009) as independent risk factors for
advanced ﬁbrosis. When steatosis was included into the
model older age (OR: 6.063, CI 95%: 3.210–11.452;
P < 0.001), PNPLA3 (OR: 2.725, CI 95%: 1.062–6.993;
P = 0.037) and low cholesterol (OR: 0.991, CI 95%:
0.984–0.998; P = 0.008) remained independent risk
factors (Table 3).
Factors associated with treatment response
Overall, 56.1% (n = 268/478) of the patients included
achieved an SVR and 24.3% (n = 116/478) had an RVR.
In a multivariate logistic regression analysis, RVR was
independently associated with younger age (<40 years;
OR: 2.810, CI 95%: 1.570–5.031; P = 0.001), low base-
line viral load (<800.000 IU/ml; OR: 6.361, CI 95%:
3.288–12.306; P < 0.001) and IL28B CC genotype (OR:
7.481, CI 95%: 3.993–14.015; P < 0.001). Steatosis had
no impact on RVR rates [G0–1: 23.8% (n = 77/324);
G2–3: 19.4% (n = 7/36) respectively; P = 0.680].
In the overall study population, SVR was indepen-
dently associated with younger age (OR: 3.264, CI 95%:
2.011–5.298; P < 0.001), low baseline viral load (OR:
2.093, CI 95%: 1.347–3.252; P = 0.001) and the IL28B

P < 0.001), low viral load (OR: 2.095, CI 95%: 1.263–
3.475, P = 0.004), the IL28B CC genotype (OR: 8.285,
CI 95%: 4.541–15.116, P < 0.001) and no/mild steatosis
(OR: 3.116, CI 95%: 1.334–7.282, P = 0.009) were inde-
pendent predictors for SVR (Table 4).

Discussion
The novel ﬁnding of this study is the role of FDFT1
polymorphism, a recently described genetic factor asso-
ciated with progression to NASH in patients with
non-alcoholic steatosis (SNP rs2645424 in FDFT1)6 on
ﬁbrosis progression in non-steatotic chronic hepatitis C
patients. The presence and extent of steatosis are impor-
tant predictors of response to treatment of chronic

hepatitis C with peg-interferon/ribavirin (15). Fat accu-
mulation in hepatocytes is of multifactorial origin.
Beyond nutritional and metabolic factors, genetic modi-
ﬁers (including PNPLA3), HCV genotype 3 (16), copper
toxicity and several drugs and toxins (including etha-
nol) can lead to steatosis.
FDFT1 encodes for the squalene synthase which
catalyzes the production of squalene from farnesyl
pyrophosphate as the ﬁrst step in the cholesterol
biosynthesis. The role of the minor allele in cholesterin
synthesis is unknown. Assuming that, it enhances cho-
lesterol
synthesis,
hepatic
cholesterol
accumulation
might play a role in the progression from steatosis to
NASH by sensitizing hepatocytes to tumour necrosis
factor- and Fas-induced apoptosis (9, 17, 18). In the
overall population, FDFT1 had no effect on the degree
of steatosis and ﬁbrosis as well as on treatment outcome
in patients with chronic hepatitis C. However, in the
subgroup of patients without steatosis, advanced ﬁbrosis
was strongly associated with AA homozygosity. Of
course, our study was not designed to investigate the
pathogenetic mechanisms between FDFT1 genotype and
ﬁbrosis. We assume that – at least in non-steatotic
patients – progression to advanced ﬁbrosis might be
partly triggered by increased free cholesterol levels in the
liver which may not be histologically apparent as macro-
or microversicular steatosis. Interestingly, high choles-
terol intake results in stellate cell activation and ﬁbrosis
(19, 20) while suppression of cholesterol synthesis with
HMG-Coenzyme A reductase inhibitors (statins) ame-
liorates ﬁbrosis (21). In patients with steatosis cofound-
ers like BMI, alcohol intake and PNPLA3 genotype
might blunt these effects.
Our study reconﬁrmed the association of SNP
rs738409 in the PNPLA3 gene and the development of
steatosis and advanced ﬁbrosis (3, 4). Carriers of the GG
allele had more than 3.6-fold risk to develop moderate
or severe steatosis (G2-3) compared to patients carrying
the C allele. Similar to the study of Tillmann et al. (10),
steatosis was also signiﬁcantly lower in patients carrying
the beneﬁcial CC allele in IL28B, but this difference
disappeared, when the data were entered into a multi-
variate model. As expected and similar to previously
published data (22), IL28B had no impact on ﬁbrosis
progression and development of cirrhosis in our study
cohort.

In line with previous studies (23, 24) IL28B CC geno-
type was strongly associated with treatment response. In
contrast, neither PNPLA3 nor FDFT1 polymorphisms
were predictors of SVR in the overall cohort, but may
have some role in some distinct subgroups. Valenti et al.
(5) showed an association of PNPLA3 GG and impaired
treatment response in difﬁcult-to-cure GT1/4 patients.
In our cohort, we were not able to conﬁrm this associa-
tion. This might be because of the relatively low number
of patients homozygous for the G allele in our study.
The impact of PNPLA3 and FDFT1 on treatment
response needs to be further clariﬁed. Genetic factors
alone are certainly not the primary causes of steatosis
and ﬁbrosis, and do not fully explain different treatment
responses. The role of alcohol abuse as cofactor for
disease progression in chronic hepatitis C is well estab-
lished (25, 26) Furthermore, PNPLA3 genotype may
even exert a differential effect on liver damaging accord-
ing to the amount of daily alcohol intake. Two studies
showed (27, 28) that development of steatosis in CHC
patients was only associated with PNPLA3 in abstainers.
In contrast, progression to cirrhosis was associated with
PNPLA3 in both subgroups (abstainers and at-risk
drinkers). In our clinic, we do not consider patients
with ongoing alcohol abuse for antiviral therapy but we
have not documented if and how much alcoholic bever-
ages were consumed in the time before patients were
referred. Thus, the lack of reliable anamnestic data did
not allow to investigate this aspect in our patient cohort.
This problem may, however, be common for most of
the treatment studies in patients with hepatitis C.
The strengths of this study were the inclusion of a
homogenous group of Caucasian patients with well-
characterized liver histology using validated scoring
systems for ﬁbrosis and steatosis. The limitations of this
study are the lack of reliable data on alcohol consump-
tion and the retrospective analysis.
In summary, FDFT1 polymorphism may have a role
for differences in ﬁbrosis progression in chronic hepati-
tis C patients without impacting on hepatic fat accumu-
lation.
